title: patching a puncture, where the disqualifier matters more than any figure
why: A home job with almost no numbers in it, which is exactly why it is worth compiling: the thing that makes it safe is not a tolerance but a refusal. A cut in the sidewall must never be patched however good the patch looks, and a procedure that does not carry that as a disqualifier will happily record a beautifully executed repair on a tyre that is going to fail.

shop.trade: one person looking after their own ride at home, no workshop
shop.machines: a Segway Xyber e-bike, plus a couple of ordinary bicycles
shop.stakes: it gets ridden in city traffic and on gravel; a brake or a tyre letting go at speed puts the rider under a car

facts.what the job is: find the puncture, patch the tube or plug the tubeless tyre, get it back on and pumped up
facts.how I find it: pump it up and listen, or put it in water and watch for bubbles
facts.what I do to the tube: rough the area up, glue, patch, press it down hard and leave it a few minutes before I put it back
facts.what stops the job dead: if the hole is in the sidewall rather than the tread, that tyre is scrap. You cannot patch a sidewall, it flexes too much and it will blow. Same if the tread is split rather than punctured
facts.how I know it worked: pump it back up, leave it, and check it is still up an hour later
facts.what pressure: same as always, whatever is printed on the sidewall of that tyre
facts.evidence I keep: photo of what came out of the tyre, the thorn or the glass or whatever, and a photo of the patch before the tyre goes back on
